newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: DE BEERS SEES '97 SALES DOWN IN DLR TERMS.
newsitem.headline: DE BEERS SEES '97 SALES DOWN IN DLR TERMS.

text.p: De Beers Consolidated Mines Ltd said on Tuesday it expected 1997 diamond sales to maintain at 1996 levels in local currency terms but sales would be down in dollar terms.

De Beers said in a statement with its half-year results that the retail market was mixed with continuing strength in the United States being offset by weakness in Japan and in those countries -- particularly in South East Asia, which were adversely affected by the strength of the dollar.
"The current expectation was that sales would be maintained at 1996 levels in local currencies but would be down in dollar terms.
"The combined results for the full year would depend on the extent to which the CSO was able to maintain the increased market share it achieved in the first half," De Beers said.

De Beers said the Central Selling Organisation (CSO)'s record first half sales of $2.88 billion coupled with the change in its own intake of diamonds compared with the first half of 1996, when it was buying both Russian and Australian diamonds under contract, had resulted in a reduction of stocks and in long and medium term liabilities.
It also led to an increase in net current assets.
De Beers said the latter half of last year saw increased competition for smaller near gem quality diamonds with increased Russian stockpile sales and Australian independent marketing.

"The price adjustments to market levels in this area enabled the CSO to sell significant quantities of these diamonds but did have an impact on trading margins which was reflected in the (De Beers) Centenary account," De Beers said.
It said further discussions with Russian authorities were required before reaching finality in the protracted negotiations with Russia over a diamond trading deal.
The company said the CSO had purchased about $150 million worth of Russian diamonds in Moscow in the first half of 1997 on a non-contractual basis.
"Procedural delays had prevented the immediate export of these diamonds, but approximately half of this amount had since been received in London".
